content: Phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidylethanolamine, and phosphatidylinositol are key components of lecithin. Lecithin was first isolated in 1846 by the French chemist and pharmacist Theodore Gobley. In 1850, Gobley named phosphatidylcholine lécithine, derived from the Ancient Greek word lekithos, meaning egg yolk, as he initially isolated lecithin from egg yolk. By 1874, Gobley had determined the complete chemical formula of phosphatidylcholine and demonstrated the presence of lecithin in various biological materials, including venous blood, bile, human brain tissue, fish eggs, fish roe, and the brains of chickens and sheep. Lecithin can be extracted chemically using solvents such as hexane, ethanol, acetone, petroleum ether, or benzene, or mechanically. It is commonly sourced from soybeans, eggs, milk, marine sources, rapeseed, cottonseed, and sunflower. While lecithin has low solubility in water, it is an excellent emulsifier. In aqueous solutions, its phospholipids can form liposomes, bilayer sheets, micelles, or lamellar structures depending on hydration and temperature. This amphipathic nature makes lecithin a versatile surfactant. Lecithin is sold as a food supplement and for medical purposes. In cooking, it is used as an emulsifier and to prevent sticking, such as in nonstick cooking sprays. As a food additive, lecithin provides dietary sources of active compounds like choline and its metabolites, which are essential for physiological functions such as cell membrane signaling, cholinergic neurotransmission, and serving as a major source of methyl groups via its metabolite, trimethylglycine (betaine). Phosphatidylcholine, a major component of lecithin, is found in all cellular organisms and is a key part of the phospholipid portion of cell membranes. Although lecithin is a source of dietary fats, the small amounts typically used as a food additive do not contribute significantly to fat intake. Commercial lecithin, used by food manufacturers, is a mixture of phospholipids in oil. It is obtained by water degumming the extracted oil of seeds, with soybean oil being a major source. Sunflower oil is also increasingly used. The main phospholipids in lecithin from soy and sunflower include phosphatidylcholine (PC), phosphatidylinositol (PI), phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), and phosphatidic acid (PA). Purified phospholipids are commercially produced for various applications. Hydrolyzed lecithin is modified enzymatically to improve its performance for specific products. In this process, a portion of the phospholipids has one fatty acid removed by phospholipase, typically phospholipase A2, which removes the fatty acid at the C2 position of glycerol. These modified phospholipids are called lysophospholipids. Lecithin can also be modified through fractionation, where it is mixed with ethanol. Phosphatidylcholine dissolves well in ethanol, while other phospholipids do not. The ethanol is then separated and evaporated to produce a phosphatidylcholine-enriched lecithin fraction. Genetically modified (GM) crops are a source of lecithin. Due to the high level of processing, GM proteins or DNA from the original crop are often undetectable in the final product, making it indistinguishable from lecithin derived from non-GM crops. However, consumer concerns about GM foods have led to regulatory changes, such as the European Union's 2000 regulation requiring labeling of food containing additives derived from GMOs, including lecithin. To comply, manufacturers must use a meticulous system of identity preservation (IP). Lecithin has emulsification and lubricant properties and acts as a surfactant. It is fully metabolized by humans, making it well-tolerated and non-toxic when ingested. This contrasts with some other emulsifiers, which are excreted via the kidneys. Commercial soybean-derived lecithin typically contains 33–35% soybean oil, 20–21% inositol phosphatides, 19–21% phosphatidylcholine, 8–20% phosphatidylethanolamine, 5–11% other phosphatides, 5% free carbohydrates, 2–5% sterols, and 1% moisture. Lecithin is used in human food, animal feed, pharmaceuticals, paints, and other industrial applications. In the pharmaceutical industry, it serves as a wetting and stabilizing agent, a choline enrichment carrier, and aids in emulsification and encapsulation. It is used in intravenous fat infusions and therapeutic applications. In animal feed, it enriches fat and protein content and improves pelletization. In the paint industry, lecithin forms protective coatings, acts as an antioxidant, prevents rust, intensifies color, and serves as a dispersing and stabilizing agent. It prevents hard settling of pigments, eliminates foam in water-based paints, and aids in the dispersion of latex-based paints. Lecithin is also used as a release agent for plastics, an anti-sludge additive in motor lubricants, and an emulsifier in textiles, rubber, and other industries. As a food additive, lecithin is non-toxic and widely used in food preparation. It acts as a natural emulsifier and lubricant. In confectionery, it reduces viscosity, replaces more expensive ingredients, controls sugar crystallization, and improves the flow properties of chocolate. It enhances the homogeneous mixing of ingredients, improves shelf life, and can be used as a coating. In emulsions and fat spreads, it stabilizes emulsions, reduces spattering during frying, and improves texture and flavor release. In doughs and bakery products, it reduces fat and egg requirements, stabilizes fermentation, increases volume, protects yeast cells in frozen dough, and acts as a releasing agent to prevent sticking. Lecithin is also used in cocoa powder to control dust and ensure complete dispersion in water. It prevents the separation of cocoa and cocoa butter in candy bars and is a component of cooking sprays to prevent sticking. In margarines with high fat content, lecithin acts as an anti-spattering agent during shallow frying. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved lecithin for human consumption, designating it as generally recognized as safe (GRAS). The European Union also approves lecithin as a food additive, designated as E322. Research indicates that soy-derived lecithin can lower serum cholesterol and triglycerides while increasing HDL (good cholesterol) levels in rats. However, clinical studies on humans have shown mixed results. While lecithin has shown benefits in improving liver function and reducing cholesterol, studies on its effects in dementia and dyskinesias have found no significant benefits. La Leche League recommends lecithin to prevent blocked milk ducts, which can lead to mastitis in breastfeeding women. Egg-derived lecithin is highly purified and typically free of allergy-causing egg proteins, making it safe for individuals with egg allergies. It is also not a concern for those on low-cholesterol diets, as lecithin in eggs inhibits cholesterol absorption. Emerging evidence suggests that lecithin is converted by gut bacteria into trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO), which enters circulation and may contribute to atherosclerosis and heart attacks over time. Soy-derived lecithin is considered kitniyot and is prohibited during Passover for Ashkenazi Jews but not at other times. Sephardi Jews, who do not have the same restrictions on rice and kitniyot during Passover, are not affected. For Muslims, lecithin is permissible if derived from plants, egg yolks, or animals slaughtered according to halal rules.
